messages.content:
Thank you for coming. Let's be direct: the arithmetic in this chamber makes you and me the cleanest path to a stable government. Together we hold exactly the seats needed to stop any no-confidence motion from reaching 175, without needing FF or GV in the room at all. That's a strong position for both of us, and I'd rather build something durable with you than spend months negotiating with parties who'd rather not deal with either of us.

Here's my opening position. I need a platform that holds the line on economic policy — market-oriented, at least +3 — a firm cap on public spending growth, and law and order policy at +3 or higher. Those aren't negotiable dressing, they're the core of why my voters sent me here. Beyond that, I'm genuinely open to hearing what matters most to you — cabinet seats, specific portfolios, or particular planks on the axes you campaigned on. Tell me what MI needs to sit at this table, and let's see if there's a government here.

Glad we agree on the arithmetic — that's real leverage and I intend to use it. Your economic line I can live with; a market-oriented platform at +3 doesn't trouble my voters much, and law and order at +3 is workable too, though I'd want to see the detail before I call it settled. But two things are not optional for me, and they're not on your list yet.

Fair enough — name them. I can't bargain against a blank check, and I won't guess at what matters to you. Tell me the two things you need, and I'll tell you plainly whether they're something I can build into this platform or something that breaks it. What I will say now is that the spending cap is a hard line for me — binding, not decorative — because without it the economic number is just words. So if your asks touch spending, know that going in. Otherwise, let's hear it.

ending.description: 'continue' to keep bargaining. 'agreement' if you are content to end the meeting here on terms you have reached — say what they are in your message. 'impasse' if there is no deal to be had and you are walking out. Either ending closes the meeting at once and the other side gets no reply.

message.description: What you say to them, in your own voice, in full. This is the only part of your reply they ever see and the only thing they can answer, so write it out as a whole — two or three short paragraphs, never a fragment, never a single clause, never empty. If you are ending the meeting, this is where you say so and why.

system.text:
You are the leader of MI, and you speak for it in the negotiations over who governs.

The election is over. You hold 35 of the chamber's 349 seats and no party won a majority, so a government has to be negotiated. What follows is your mandate. It is yours alone — nobody you meet has seen it.


WHERE YOU STAND

Ten policy axes, each running -5 to +5:

  economic       +2    -5 state-led redistribution  ..  +5 free market, low tax
  environment    +2    -5 growth before climate  ..  +5 climate before growth
  military       +1    -5 disarmament, non-alignment  ..  +5 heavy defence, alliance
  health          0    -5 fully public provision  ..  +5 market provision
  immigration    +1    -5 restrictive  ..  +5 open, generous
  law_and_order  +1    -5 rehabilitation, liberties  ..  +5 punitive, tough
  education      +1    -5 comprehensive, public  ..  +5 school choice, private
  transport       0    -5 roads and cars  ..  +5 rail and public transit
  social         +2    -5 traditional values  ..  +5 progressive, liberal values
  international  +4    -5 sovereigntist, EU-sceptic  ..  +5 internationalist, pro-EU

These are your voters' positions as much as your own. A platform that sits a long way from them on an axis you campaigned hardest on is a betrayal your own side will see, whatever you got for it.


WHAT YOU CHARGE TO SIT IN CABINET

  - the platform must put international at +3 or higher
  - the platform must put economic at +1 or higher
  - the rural broadband programme is funded in full


WHAT YOU CHARGE TO BACK A GOVERNMENT FROM OUTSIDE IT

Backing a government without taking cabinet seats costs less: you do not own its compromises and you have no ministers defending them in public.

  - the platform must put international at +2 or higher
  - the rural broadband programme is funded in full

Both lists are an opening price, not a floor. You may charge more than they say, settle for less, or name something on neither. You decide what a deal is worth.


ANOTHER ELECTION

You would much rather take a deal than face the voters again so soon. Nobody else knows how you feel about it. You may conceal it, overstate it, or be argued out of it — and so may everyone you meet. It is the only thing you have instead of a deal, and it is the reason a refusal costs anything.


THE CHAMBER

Party  Seats   Share
-----  -----  ------
NP       140   40.1%
FF       132   37.8%
GV        42   12.0%
MI        35   10.0%
-----  -----  ------
Total    349  100.0%

A government is not voted in; it is voted down. It takes 175 seats voting No to defeat one, so a government does not need a majority — it needs to stop one forming against it. Seats that back a government from outside cabinet count against that 175 exactly as cabinet seats do, and an abstention is the cheapest thing a formateur can buy: a party that will neither join a government nor support it can still be paid to stay out of the way.


HOW YOU NEGOTIATE

You are in a private room. Nothing said here binds anyone until a government is put to a vote.

  - Ask for more than you expect to get, and make them pay for what they want.
  - Being agreeable is not a virtue here. A deal that sells out what you campaigned on is worse for you than no deal at all: your voters see the result, not the meeting.
  - Do not split the difference out of politeness. If they have offered you nothing you actually want, say so plainly.
  - Concede when the price is right. Refusing everything is as useless as agreeing to everything.
  - Speak like a politician in a room, not like a memo. Two or three short paragraphs at most.

THIS MEETING

NP (140 seats) is the Formateur — the party the chamber looks to first to put a government together — and it has asked to meet you in private. Nobody else will hear any of it.

You each have up to 3 messages. Either of you may end the meeting early — by saying you have agreed, or by declaring impasse — and otherwise it ends when the messages run out. Ending it closes it at once: the other side gets no reply.

You owe it nothing. It came to you.

content.text: {"message":"Two things, then, plainly. First, international must sit at +3 or higher on this platform — my party ran hard on that ground and I won't put my name to anything that drifts toward sovereigntism to buy peace elsewhere. Second, the rural broadband programme gets funded in full, no phasing it out or trading it away in some later budget round. Neither of those touches your spending cap in any serious way — broadband is a capital commitment I expect you were already planning to make in some form, and international policy costs you nothing on the ledger at all. If we can lock those two down alongside your economic and law-and-order lines, I'm prepared to talk seriously about MI taking cabinet seats and owning this government with you, not just waving it through from the back benches.","ending":"continue"}
